subject: Reporting fit statistics when using a robust test

messages.author: 4dfb10f1208d18ea
messages.subject: Reporting fit statistics when using a robust test
parts:
Hello,

After testing various models with MLM estimation and robust standard errors to adjust for non-normality of some variables, I get two outputs for my fit values. The regular "ML" and then the "Robust". I suppose that the "robust" column provides the results of using robust standard errors, and I would like to report those. However, the fitmeasures() function only returns the "ML" results. In addition, if I want to compare two nested models with lavTestLRT(), it seems that it also only accounts for the "ML" results. In this second case I suppose that it should be less worrisome if we base our model comparison on equivalent non-robust results. 
Any light on this would be appreciated,

Arno

On Monday, January 23, 2017 at 11:45:31 AM UTC+1, Arno Polegato wrote:
Hello,

After testing various models with MLM estimation and robust standard errors to adjust for non-normality of some variables, I get two outputs for my fit values. The regular "ML" and then the "Robust". I suppose that the "robust" column provides the results of using robust standard errors, and I would like to report those.

When you request robust SEs, those are the only SEs reported in the summary() output or parameterEstimates() output.  There are not separate columns for "naïve" and "robust" SEs of estimated parameters.
However, the fitmeasures() function only returns the "ML" results.

The robust SEs are not used to adjust ("scale") the chi-squared statistic, but fitMeasures() should return naïve test values (labeled "chisq", "df", and "pvalue") as well as robust ones using the scaled test statistic (labeled "chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", and "pvalue.scaled").
In addition, if I want to compare two nested models with lavTestLRT()

That function will first check whether you requested a robust test statistic (or used a shortcut like estimator = "mlm"), and then apply the appropriate robust test.  That does not involved taking the difference between scaled test statistics.  Instead, it takes the difference between the naïve test statistics, then scales that to account for nonnormality..
